text_pairs.original: The tradeoffs in `fibonacci(n)` are grounded in time–space complexity, recurrence relations, and dynamic programming. A naïve recursive definition mirrors the mathematical recurrence \(F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2)\) but causes exponential recomputation, while memoization or tabulation exploits overlapping subproblems to reduce time to \(O(n)\) at the cost of extra memory; matrix exponentiation and fast doubling further use linear algebra and divide-and-conquer to achieve \(O(\log n)\) time.

text_pairs.original: Open problems remain in making Fibonacci implementations both asymptotically optimal and practically safe across environments: fast-doubling and matrix methods are efficient, but handling very large `n` still raises issues around big-integer multiplication cost, memory pressure, and overflow behavior in fixed-width languages. There are also unresolved engineering questions in selecting the best strategy adaptively—iteration, memoization, closed-form approximation, or fast-doubling—based on input size, precision requirements, recursion limits, and hardware characteristics without introducing correctness risks from floating-point error or implementation complexity.
